chunks: "The difference is what the controller changes to regulate. In PWM the switching frequency is fixed and the controller changes the duty cycle, so the pulse width tracks the load.
In PFM the pulses are all the same size, a fixed peak current or a fixed on-time, and the controller regulates by changing how often it fires.
At light load it fires rarely and sleeps in between. That leads to the trade-offs.
PWM has a clean, predictable spectrum at one frequency and its harmonics, so filtering and EMI are easy, the ripple is small and the transient response is fast because the loop is always running.
But it burns gate drive and switch-node charging loss every cycle, so light-load efficiency is poor: tens of percent at milliamps. PFM reverses that.
Switching losses scale with the pulse rate, which scales with the load, so efficiency stays around 90 percent from a few hundred microamps up.

But the ripple is larger and low frequency, it varies with load and can land in the audio band, the spectrum is smeared so EMI filtering is harder, and the converter needs time to wake up when the load jumps.
So I use PFM when battery life at idle dominates, and PWM when noise or transient response does, and most ICs switch between them by load, with a forced-PWM pin for noise-sensitive rails."
